{{DISPLAYTITLE:What a proof assistant does}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/Elaboration|Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A '''proof assistant''' is a program that checks proofs written in a formal
language, step by step, while a person writes them. Lean is one. This page says
what such a program does, how it differs from a program that looks for proofs on
its own, which other systems do the same work, and what it means, and does not
mean, when a proof assistant says that a proof is checked.

== A language with no gaps ==

A proof in a journal is written for a reader. It skips steps the reader can be
trusted to fill in, and it relies on conventions the reader already shares. That
is efficient, and it is also where mistakes hide: a step that looks routine may
not be.

A proof assistant has no shared conventions to fall back on. Everything is
written in a '''formal language''', a notation with fixed rules for what counts as
a statement and what counts as a valid step. Each step must be justified by a rule
of the logic, by a definition, or by a theorem already proved, and each of those
in turn rests on earlier ones, down to a short list of basic rules and
axioms.<ref name="tpil-intro">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, with contributions from the Lean Community, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', chapter 1, "Introduction", online book for Lean 4.33.0. [https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Introduction/ lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Introduction/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> Nothing is taken as obvious.

This makes formal proofs much longer than written ones, and much more tedious to
produce by hand.<ref name="geuvers2009">Herman Geuvers, "Proof assistants: history, ideas and future", ''Sādhanā'' 34 (1), 2009, pp. 3–25. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s12046-009-0001-5 doi:10.1007/s12046-009-0001-5]</ref> A proof assistant exists to make that work manageable and to
check the result.

== Interactive ==

The word ''assistant'' describes how the work is done. A person states a theorem
and starts to prove it. At each point the program shows what is still to be
proved, called the '''goal''', and the facts available for proving it. The person
supplies a step. The program either accepts the step and shows the new goal, or
refuses it and says why. The work ends when no goal is left. The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Holes and goals|holes and goals]] shows this
exchange in Lean.

The person does not have to write every tiny step. Most proof assistants offer
commands, called [[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Tactics|tactics]], that carry
out many small steps at once: split a statement into cases, rewrite with an
equation, try a standard argument. Whatever a tactic produces is still checked
before it is accepted.

Lean was started in 2013 by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research as an
interactive theorem prover, the technical name for a proof assistant.<ref name="tpil-intro" /> Lean 4 is a
reimplementation of it written in Lean itself.<ref name="lean4-cade">Leonardo de Moura and Sebastian Ullrich, "The Lean 4 theorem prover and programming language", in ''Automated Deduction – CADE 28'', Lecture Notes in Computer Science 12699, Springer, 2021, pp. 625–635. [https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 doi:10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37]</ref>

== Finding a proof and checking one ==

A computer can help with a proof in two different ways. It can '''find''' a proof,
or it can '''check''' one that someone has supplied.

'''Automated theorem provers''' are built for finding. Given a statement in a
restricted form, they search for a proof by themselves, using fixed procedures
for propositional and first-order logic and for particular kinds of problem such
as arithmetic over the integers.<ref name="tpil-intro" /> They can be very fast,
but their range is limited: one cannot set up a whole mathematical theory inside
them.<ref name="geuvers2009" /> The authors of ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4''
also note that such systems often favour speed over a guarantee that their answers
are correct, and that a fault in them can be hard to detect.<ref name="tpil-intro" />

A proof assistant is built for checking. It sets a high standard, every step
justified, and in return it asks much more of the person using
it.<ref name="tpil-intro" /> In most cases the person supplies the ideas, and the
machine supplies the bookkeeping and the verdict.<ref name="geuvers2009" />

The line is not sharp. Lean includes automation that searches for proofs of
particular kinds of statement, and the project's stated aim is to
place such tools inside a system whose final product is a fully checked
proof.<ref name="tpil-intro" /> What a search procedure finds is not trusted
because it was found; it is accepted only after it has been checked, so an honest fault
in the search can cost a proof but does not let a wrong one through.<ref name="ref-validating">The Lean Developers, "Validating a Lean proof", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0. [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/ValidatingProofs/] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Automation and its limits|automation and its limits]]
says more.

== Other proof assistants ==

Lean is one of several mature proof assistants. They differ in the logic they
check, in how a user writes proofs, and in the libraries built for them.

* '''Rocq''', called '''Coq''' until 2025, began in 1984 at INRIA-Rocquencourt in the work of Thierry Coquand and Gérard Huet. It checks proofs in a Calculus of Inductive Constructions, a type theory of the same family as Lean's.<ref name="rocq-about">The Rocq Team, "About Rocq", ''The Rocq Prover''. [https://rocq-prover.org/about rocq-prover.org/about] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref><ref name="lean4-cade" /> The change of name was completed with version 9.0 on 12 March 2025.<ref name="rocq-9">The Rocq Team, "Rocq 9.0.0", ''The Rocq Prover'', 12 March 2025. [https://rocq-prover.org/releases/9.0.0 rocq-prover.org/releases/9.0.0] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref> A proof of the four colour theorem was checked in it.<ref name="wadler2015">Philip Wadler, "Propositions as types", ''Communications of the ACM'' 58 (12), 2015, pp. 75–84. [https://doi.org/10.1145/2699407 doi:10.1145/2699407]</ref>
* '''Isabelle''' describes itself as a generic proof assistant. It was originally developed at the University of Cambridge and the Technische Universität München.<ref name="isabelle">''Isabelle'', home page. [https://isabelle.in.tum.de/ isabelle.in.tum.de] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>
* '''HOL Light''' was written by John Harrison. It is implemented in the programming language OCaml and has a much simpler logical core than other systems of its family.<ref name="hol-light">John Harrison, ''The HOL Light theorem prover'', home page. [https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~jrh13/hol-light/ www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~jrh13/hol-light/] (accessed 14 October 2026).</ref> Isabelle and HOL Light both descend from Robin Milner's LCF system of the 1970s.<ref name="geuvers2009" /> The formal proof of the Kepler conjecture was checked with the two together.<ref name="flyspeck">Thomas Hales and 21 co-authors, "A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture", ''Forum of Mathematics, Pi'' 5, e2, 2017. [https://doi.org/10.1017/fmp.2017.1 doi:10.1017/fmp.2017.1]; preprint [https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.02155 arXiv:1501.02155].</ref>
* '''Agda''' is a dependently typed programming language, an extension of Martin-Löf's type theory, which can be used as a proof assistant.<ref name="agda">The Agda Team, "What is Agda?", ''Agda documentation''. [https://agda.readthedocs.io/en/latest/getting-started/what-is-agda.html agda.readthedocs.io] (accessed 13 October 2026).</ref>

None of these is a standard that the others fall short of. The choice between
them is a choice of logic, of style and of library.

== What "checked" means ==

When Lean accepts a theorem, the claim it makes is narrow and exact. The statement
has been read according to the definitions and notation in force, and Lean's
kernel, the small part of the program that has the last word, has accepted a proof
of that statement from the definitions, theorems and axioms in the file and in the
files it imports.<ref name="ref-validating" />

That is a strong claim. It leaves out several things.

'''It does not say the statement means what its author intended.''' Lean's
reference manual separates two questions: whether a theorem has a valid proof, and
what the theorem's statement means.<ref name="ref-validating" /> The checker answers
only the first. If a definition misreads the idea it was meant to capture, the
theorem is a true statement about the wrong thing. The team that formalised the
Kepler conjecture listed this first among the questions an auditor must ask: did
the right theorem get formalised?<ref name="flyspeck" /> The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Stating the right thing|stating the right thing]]
takes this up.

'''It does not say the axioms are true.''' A proof is valid relative to the axioms
it uses. Lean can list them for any theorem; see
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What the axioms are|what the axioms are]].

'''It assumes the checker is correct.''' The part that must be trusted is kept
small on purpose, and independent checkers exist, but it is still a
program.<ref name="ref-intro">The Lean Developers, "Introduction", ''The Lean Language Reference'', for Lean 4.35.0, section 1.1, "History". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Introduction/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/Introduction/] (accessed 14 October 2026).</ref><ref name="ref-validating" /> See
[[Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What has to be trusted|what has to be trusted]].

'''It assumes honesty in what is imported.''' A check of one file trusts the
libraries it uses, unless those are checked again as well. Lean's manual describes
stronger checks, step by step, for cases where a proof may have been written to
mislead.<ref name="ref-validating" />

Within these limits, "checked" means that no step was skipped and no case was
forgotten. That is more than a careful human reader can promise, and the next page
explains why mathematics came to want it.
